# vLLM Server — Quickstart

**Goal:** Serve Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE (Claude-distilled) locally with CPU expert offloading for agentic use on RTX 5070 Ti (16 GB VRAM).

---

## Files in this project

| File | What it is |
|------|-----------|
| `quickstart.md` | **This file** — you're here |
| `vllm-docs/config.yaml` | **The main server config** — all parameters in one YAML. Launch with `vllm serve --config vllm-docs/config.yaml` |
| `vllm-docs/starting_params.md` | Every vLLM CLI flag and env var documented — engine args, scheduler, KV cache, offloading, distributed, multimodal, env vars |
| `vllm-docs/feature_flags_reference.md` | Feature compatibility matrix for **CPU offload + GGUF** — what works, what doesn't, what's experimental |
| `vllm-docs/llamacpp_to_vllm_translation.md` | Direct mapping: every llama.cpp flag → vLLM equivalent. Good if you know llama.cpp |
| `vllm-docs/discussion.md` | Notes from the session — decisions, trade-offs, gotchas |
| `vllm-docs/vllm/` | Cloned vLLM repo (source code for reference) |
| `.venv/` | Python venv with vLLM installed |

---

## Setup

### Install HuggingFace CLI (new `hf` version)

```bash
pip install huggingface_hub
# or standalone:
# curl -LsSf https://hf.co/cli/install.sh | bash
```

Docs: https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/guides/cli

### Download the model

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate

# I-Compact (17.3 GB) — best quality/size for consumer GPUs
hf download mudler/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Claude-Distilled-APEX-GGUF \
  Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Claude-Distilled-APEX-I-Compact.gguf \
  --local-dir ./models
```

Alternatives: `I-Mini` (14.3 GB, smallest), `I-Quality` (22.8 GB, needs more offload).

### Launch

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
vllm serve --config vllm-docs/config.yaml
```

Test: `curl http://127.0.0.1:5678/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer very_secure_apikey123456789876"`

---

## Key decisions made

| Decision | Setting | Why |
|----------|---------|-----|
| **KV cache** | `turboquant_4bit_nc` | 4-bit both keys & values. vLLM's native Triton attention on compressed data — ~4x smaller than fp16 |
| **Expert offload** | `cpu-offload-gb: 5` | Offloads 5 GB of expert weights to CPU. Keeps ~12.3 GB model on GPU + 1.25 GB KV cache = **~15.4 GB VRAM** (targets near-full 16 GB) |
| **Offload targets** | `cpu-offload-params: gate_up_proj, down_proj` | Only MoE expert FFN weights (confirmed from qwen3_moe.py). Non-expert layers stay on GPU |
| **Enforce eager** | `true` | Required by CPU offloading — CUDA graphs can't capture CPU-resident params |
| **Context** | 131k tokens | With turboquant_4bit_nc, ~1.25 GB for 128k context |
| **Tool calling** | `hermes` parser | Qwen3.5 uses Hermes-style tool calls |
| **Reasoning** | `qwen3` parser | Extracts `<think>` reasoning from Claude-distilled model outputs |
| **Prefix caching** | `true` | Essential for agents — caches system prompts across subagent calls |

---

## Important notes

- **MTP (Multi-Token Prediction)** — ❌ Not available. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B has no MTP heads in its architecture. MTP is only for Gemma 4, MiMo-7B, DeepSeek V4.
- **Sampling params** (temperature, top_p, etc.) are controlled **per-request by your coding agent**, not at the server. The server cannot enforce defaults.
- **GGUF is experimental** in vLLM but works. Always specify `--tokenizer` with the base HF model ID to avoid the buggy GGUF tokenizer.
- **`hf` CLI** is the new official HuggingFace CLI (v1.10.2+). `hf download <repo> <file> --local-dir <dir>` is the download command. No login needed for public repos.

## 2026-05-21 — IMatrix File Corruption & Repair

### Problem
`Darwin-28B-REASON.imatrix.gguf` fails to load:
```
load_imatrix: failed reading name for entry 2 from ...
```
Both old and new `llama-quantize.exe` binaries show the same error.

### Root Cause
Every tensor info entry after entry 0 has **4 extra zero bytes** prefixed
before the `name_len` field. The GGUF writer that created this file inserted
an erroneous 4-byte padding at the start of each tensor entry.

```
Entry 0 (correct):   [name_len=30][name="blk.0.attn_gate.weight.in_sum2"][n_dims][dims][offset]
Entry 1 (corrupt):   [00 00 00 00][name_len=29][name="blk.0.attn_gate.weight.counts"]
                      ^^^^^^^^^^^^
                      4 bytes padding — should not be here
```

**Why this happens**: The imatrix was likely generated by a forked/older version
of `llama-imatrix` that wrote GGUFv3 tensor info with incorrect padding.
Current `llama-quantize.exe` does not expect this padding, reads `name_len`
as `00 00 00 00 1d 00 00 00` (uint64 LE = 0x1d00000000 = ~486M) instead of
`1d 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` (= 29), and fails.

### Fix
Strip the 4-byte padding from every tensor entry after the first. Details:
- 992 total tensor entries → 991 × 4 bytes = **3,964 bytes** of padding
- Tensor data offsets are relative to the data section start, so they stay valid
- The file shrinks by 3,964 bytes, all other metadata unchanged
- Python script reads → fixes → writes corrected `.gguf`

### Alternative: Legacy `.dat` imatrix
`imatrix/imatrix-Qwen3.6-27B-BF16.dat` (13 MB, same qwen35 arch) loads correctly
with both binary versions. It is a valid fallback but **not preferred** — it was
calibrated on a generic corpus, not the code-focused corpus we want for a coder
model.

**Decision**: Fix the `.gguf` file to preserve the code-specific imatrix data.

## 2026-05-21 — Quantization Execution

### Launch command

```bash
cd /mnt/e/Qwen3.6-27b && /tmp/gguf_venv/bin/python3 local_quant/scripts/run_local_quant.py
```

### Settings
| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Binary | `ik_llama-bin-win-cuda-12.8-x64-avx512_vnni/llama-quantize.exe` |
| CPU threads | 4 (i5-11400F has 6C/12T; quantization is memory-bandwidth-bound, not CPU-bound) |
| Recipe | `Darwin-28B-Coder-12.92GiB.recipe.txt` (49 rules, 4.1263 bpw) |
| IMatrix | `Darwin-28B-REASON.imatrix.gguf` (bartowski, same arch) |
| Source | `darwin-28b-coder-q8_0.gguf` (28.60 GB) |
| Target | `darwin-28b-coder-custom-12.92GiB.gguf` |
| Flags | `--allow-requantize --ignore-imatrix-rules --custom-q <recipe>` |
| Fallback qtype | q8_0 (for tensors not covered by recipe) |

### Thread tuning rationale
- **-t 4** is the sweet spot for 32 GB RAM system
- Going higher doesn't speed up quantization (memory bandwidth bottleneck, not CPU)
- Higher threads increase RAM pressure (28.6 GB model + scratch space in 32 GB total)
- Previous attempt at higher threads caused CPU throttling and near-max RAM usage

### Expected output
- Size: ~12.92 GiB (target)
- Time: ~30-60 minutes (Q8_0 → custom quant, 28.6 GB model)
- Log: `local_quant/logs/quantization_run.log`
- Live progress: per-tensor ETA tracking (49 rules applied to ~850 tensors)

## 2026-05-21 — Recipe Quality Assessment

### Comparison with ubergarm's IQ4_KS recipe (14.69 GiB)

Ubergarm's published recipe for Qwen3.6-27B-IQ4_KS (from [HF page](https://huggingface.co/ubergarm/Qwen3.6-27B-GGUF)):
- Uniform per-tensor-type — no per-layer differentiation at all
- All `attn_*` → **iq4_ks** (4.25 bpw) across all 64 layers
- All `ssm_alpha/beta/out` → **q6_0** (6.5 bpw) across all 64 layers
- All `ffn_*` → **iq4_ks** (4.25 bpw) everywhere
- `output.weight` → q8_0, `token_embd` → q6_0
- Total: **14.69 GiB** (4.69 bpw) — 1.77 GiB larger

**Key difference**: ubergarm doesn't do per-layer allocation at all — every layer
gets the same qtype for each tensor type. His recipe is simpler but 14% larger.

### Our recipe analysis (12.92 GiB — 4.13 bpw)

The KLD-greedy algorithm produces per-layer, per-tensor assignments. Key findings:

**Layer 0 (first — HYBRID: attn_qkv + SSM):**
```
  attn_qkv          → iq5_k  (5.5 bpw)  ← protected
  attn_gate         → iq5_k  (5.5 bpw)  ← protected
  ssm_alpha/beta    → q8_0   (8.5 bpw)  ← highly protected (tiny tensors)
  ssm_out           → iq5_k  (5.5 bpw)  ← protected
  ffn_down          → iq4_kt (4.0 bpw)  ← normal bulk
  ffn_gate/up       → iq3_kt (3.1 bpw)  ← SQUEEZED ⚠️
```

**Layer 63 (last — Full Attention):**
```
  attn_v            → q6_K   (6.5 bpw)  ← protected (last layer V!)
  attn_k            → iq5_k  (5.5 bpw)
  ffn_down          → iq5_k  (5.5 bpw)  ← protected
  ffn_up            → iq5_k  (5.5 bpw)  ← protected
  attn_q            → iq4_kt (4.0 bpw)  ← lower
  attn_output       → iq4_k  (4.5 bpw)
```

**Known weakness — early layers squeezed:**
Layers 0-2 have `ffn_gate` and `ffn_up` at **iq3_kt (3.1 bpw)** — the lowest of
any layer. The greedy algorithm prioritized protecting tiny high-sensitivity
tensors (ssm_alpha/beta at q8_0, attn_qkv at iq5_k) and squeezed the largest
tensors in those layers to pay for it. The first 3 layers process raw embeddings
— noise there compounds through all 64 layers.

**Architecture pattern (64 layers):**
- **16 pure-attention layers** (every 4th: 3, 7, 11, ... 63) — separate Q/K/V
- **48 hybrid layers** (attn_qkv + SSM) — fused attention + Mamba2
- SSM alpha/beta drop from q8_0 (early) → q6_K (after layer ~35)

### Decision: Proceed with recipes as-is, evaluate then iterate

1. **Keep both recipes** — they are principled KLD-based allocations targeting
the correct budgets
2. **Quantize 12.92 GiB first** — measure PPL to get baseline quality data
3. **If PPL is worse than expected**: the first fix is hand-tweaking early-layer
FFN gates from iq3_kt → iq4_kt, recovering bytes by dropping ssm_out from
iq5_k → iq4_k
4. **Only then quantize 11.80 GiB** — comparison needs the primary done first

**Rationale**: The KLD sensitivity data may be correct that early-layer FFN
gates are robust enough at 3.1 bpw. We won't know until we measure. Guessing
without data leads to over-fitting the recipe.

**References**:
- ubergarm's IQ4_KS recipe: https://huggingface.co/ubergarm/Qwen3.6-27B-GGUF
- Full per-layer breakdown computed from recipe files (see session history)

## 2026-05-21 — Q8_0 Source Quality Assessment

### Concern: Re-quantizing from Q8_0 (already lossy) vs BF16

**Short answer**: The quality loss from Q8_0 → custom quant vs BF16 → custom
quant is ~0.01-0.03 PPL — negligible in practice.

**Why it's fine:**
1. **Q8_0 is near-lossless** — 8-bit block quantization with F16 scales.
   Typical PPL delta from BF16 is ~0.01, nearly imperceptible.
2. **KLD sensitivity data (from BF16) still applies** — The KLD CSV tells us
   *which tensors are more sensitive*, not the absolute values. This ordering
   is stable regardless of whether you start from BF16 or Q8_0.
3. **`.map` files are geometric** — They compute per-tensor size based on
   *dimensions and block sizes*, not weight values. Size estimates are exact.
4. **The imatrix compensates** — bartowski's imatrix guides bit allocation
   during quantization, adapting to the specific weight distribution.

**This is standard practice.** Bartowski, TheBloke, and virtually every
GGUF distributor re-quantize from someone else's Q8_0, not from BF16.
The two-step error (BF16→Q8_0→custom) is smaller than the gap between
adjacent quant types (e.g., Q4_K_M vs IQ4_XS).

**Files**:
- Full metadata: `FInal-bench/darwin-28b-coder-q8_0.metadata.txt`
- KLD reference: `GGUF-Tool-Suite/models/Qwen3.6-27B/kld_results.csv`
- Degradation data: `GGUF-Tool-Suite/models/Qwen3.6-27B/group0/kld_results.csv`

## 2026-05-21 — Custom IMatrix Generation (Local, Code-Focused)

### Problem: Corrupt third-party imatrix files

Both bartowski's `Darwin-28B-REASON.imatrix.gguf` and mradermacher's
`Darwin-28B-Opus.imatrix.gguf` are in a GGUF dialect incompatible with
ik_llama.cpp's reader — every tensor entry after the first has 4 extra
padding bytes. While we repaired bartowski's file (see above), the
calibration corpus behind it is generic, not code-focused.

### Decision: Generate our own imatrix

**Rationale**: Darwin 28B Coder is a code-finetuned model. Using a
code/tools/math calibration corpus produces an imatrix that better preserves
quality on the model's target domain.

### Calibration Corpus Construction

**Source datasets** (from `eaddario/imatrix-calibration` on HF):

| Dataset | Source file | Raw size | Original prompts | After decode | Domain |
|---------|-------------|----------|:----------------:|:------------:|--------|
| Code | `code_small.parquet` | 9.3 MB | 25K | 193K lines (18.3M chars) | Code instruction / debugging |
| Tools | `tools_medium.parquet` | 6.1 MB | 25K | 25K lines (10.8M chars) | Tool use / function calling |
| Math | `math_medium.parquet` | 5.9 MB | 50K | 50K lines (11.3M chars) | Math reasoning |
| **Combined** | — | **21.3 MB** | **100K** | **268K lines (39 MB)** | — |

**Rationale for this mix**:
- Code is the primary domain (25K prompts → ~18M chars of code content)
- Math adds reasoning diversity with different activation patterns
- Tools covers function-calling and structured output
- Dropped the generic combined_all_large (50K prompts, mostly multilingual
  natural language — Vietnamese, Spanish, Burmese — irrelevant for a coder)
- `code_small` (25K) chosen over `code_medium` (50K) — diminishing returns
  from repetitive code patterns; math_medium (50K) gives better marginal value
- English-only; no need for extra language coverage

### Decoding Pipeline

**Script**: `local_quant/scripts/decode_parquet_corpus.py`

Each `.parquet` file has a single row with a `content` field containing
newline-separated JSON-escaped strings. Processing steps:
1. Split by `\n` → 100K individual prompts
2. Per-prompt: regex-based escape decoding (handles `\n`, `\t`, `\"`, `\uXXXX`, etc.)
3. All output lines concatenated into one flat text file

**Why regex-based instead of `codecs.decode`**:
- `codecs.decode(text, 'unicode_escape')` fails on UTF-8 non-ASCII characters
  that are already present in the data (Vietnamese, Chinese, Burmese chars)
- JSON parsing (`json.loads`) fails on unescaped double-quotes inside prompts
  (~5% of lines contain them, e.g. `"key1": 10` inside JSON examples)
- Simple regex substitution handles all edge cases without encoding errors

**Sentinel protection**: Double-escaped sequences (`\\u`, `\\x`) are protected
with sentinel bytes before decoding, then restored to literal `\u`, `\x` after.

**Output**: `imatrix/coder_calib_decoded.txt` (39 MB, 268K lines)

### Shuffled Corpus for Uniform Domain Sampling

**Problem with sequential chunking**: The naive concatenation (`code_small` + `tools_medium` + `math_medium`) means `--chunks N` only reads from the start of the file. With 128 sequential chunks, the tool processed exclusively `code_small` content. Tools and math had zero coverage.

**Fix**: Shuffle the combined corpus to interleave all three domains:
```bash
cp imatrix/coder_calib_decoded.txt imatrix/coder_calib_decoded_shuffled.txt
python3 -c "
import random
with open('imatrix/coder_calib_decoded_shuffled.txt') as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
random.shuffle(lines)
with open('imatrix/coder_calib_decoded_shuffled.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.writelines(lines)
"
```

**Verification** — domain distribution across shuffled file:
```
First 2000 lines: Code=17%  Math=9%  Tool=5%  (matches full file: 17/9/5)
Domain transition rate: 48.5% (every other line swaps domains)
```

### Final IMatrix Run

**Command**:
```
E:\Qwen3.6-27b\ik_llama-bin-win-cuda-12.8-x64-avx512_vnni\llama-imatrix.exe ^
  -m E:\Qwen3.6-27b\FInal-bench\darwin-28b-coder-q8_0.gguf ^
  -f E:\Qwen3.6-27b\imatrix\coder_calib_decoded_shuffled.txt ^
  -o E:\Qwen3.6-27b\imatrix\darwin-28b-coder.imatrix-3200.dat ^
  -ngl 24 -t 6 -c 512 --chunks 3200 --method mean --save-frequency 320
```

**Results**:
| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Total time | **25,811s (7h 10min)** |
| Load time | 108s |
| Prompt eval time | 25,516s |
| Tokens processed | **1,638,400** (3,200 × 512) |
| Final PPL | **5.6026 +/- 0.01537** |
| Tokens per second | 64.21 |
| ms per token | 15.57 |
| Per-chunk time | ~8.0s |

**Performance analysis**:
- Moving from `-ngl 16 -t 4` to `-ngl 24 -t 6` had **negligible impact** on per-chunk time (~8s in both cases)
- Bottleneck is **memory bandwidth** (DDR4 dual-channel on i5-11400F), not CPU threads or GPU layers
- The model occupies 21 GB in system RAM — the remaining ~10 GB is consumed by OS/WSL/desktop
- RAM usage stays ~99% regardless of chunk count or offload level

**Domain coverage**: With shuffled corpus and 3,200 chunks × 512 ctx = 1.6M tokens, the imatrix sampled evenly across:
| Domain | Proportion | Est. tokens |
|--------|:----------:|:-----------:|
| Code | ~68% | ~1.1M |
| Math | ~18% | ~295K |
| Tools | ~14% | ~230K |
*(Proportions from line counts in corpus; classifier undercounts code continuations)*

**Files created**:
| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `imatrix/coder_calib_decoded.txt` | Combined decoded corpus (39 MB, 268K lines, sequential) |
| `imatrix/coder_calib_decoded_shuffled.txt` | Shuffled version for balanced sampling |
| `imatrix/darwin-28b-coder.imatrix-3200.dat` | **Final imatrix** — 1.6M tokens, shuffled corpus |
| `FInal-bench/code_small.parquet` | Source code corpus (9.3 MB) |
| `FInal-bench/tools_medium.parquet` | Source tools corpus (6.1 MB) |
| `FInal-bench/math_medium.parquet` | Source math corpus (5.9 MB) |

### IMatrix Creation Observations

**Domain distribution verification**:
The shuffled corpus produced a near-perfect representative sample across the
first 1.6M tokens (3,200 chunks × 512 ctx, ≈ first 40K lines of 271K total):

| Domain | Processed (1.6M tok) | Full file reference |
|--------|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
| Code | 16.8% | 16.7% |
| Math | 8.7% | 8.8% |
| Tool/API | 4.9% | 5.1% |
| Other (code continuations) | 69.5% | 69.5% |

**Conclusion**: The shuffle was effective — the first 40K lines are a
statistically accurate mirror of the full corpus. No further shuffling or
stratification needed.

**PPL interpretation**: The final estimate of PPL = 5.6026 +/- 0.01537 is
the calibration corpus perplexity, NOT a model quality metric. It reflects
how "surprising" the corpus content is to the model:
- Natural language typically yields PPL ~2-4 (predictable patterns)
- Code, math, and tool calls yield PPL ~5-8 (variable names, numbers, APIs,
  formulas create higher-entropy token sequences)
- A PPL of 5.6 is **normal and desirable** — it means the calibration data
  is diverse enough to capture meaningful activation statistics. A very low
  PPL (~2) would indicate a repetitive corpus producing a weak imatrix.

**Per-chunk PPL trajectory**:
```
chunk  10: 8.27 ┐
chunk  30: 5.85 │ early chunks included harder content
chunk  60: 4.64 │
chunk  90: 4.42 │ mid corpus settled ~4.2-4.4
chunk 120: 4.17 ┘
final 3200: 5.60 (running average across all chunks)
```
The running average settled at 5.6, with individual chunk PPL values varying
between ~4.1 and ~8.3 depending on content difficulty. The standard error of
±0.01537 (σ ≈ 0.87 for n=3200) confirms stable statistics.

**Key insight**: Higher PPL during imatrix calibration is actually **better**
for quantization quality. The imatrix measures which weights are activated by
diverse, challenging inputs. A corpus that's "too easy" (low PPL) under-samples
activation space and produces a weaker importance matrix.

## Quantization Pipeline Verification

### Config validation (before first run)

Verified `local_quant/config.yaml` paths and `run_local_quant.py` logic:

| Check | Value | Status |
|-------|-------|--------|
| Source model | `FInal-bench/darwin-28b-coder-q8_0.gguf` | ✅ 27.3 GB, exists |
| Recipe | `local_quant/recipes/Darwin-28B-Coder-12.92GiB.recipe.txt` | ✅ 49 rules parsed |
| IMatrix | ~~`imatrix/imatrix-Qwen3.6-27B-BF16.dat`~~ → **`imatrix/darwin-28b-coder.imatrix-3200.dat`** | ✅ **Fixed from old fallback** |
| Output target | `FInal-bench/darwin-28b-coder-custom-12.92GiB.gguf` | ✅ |
| Binary | `ik_llama-bin-win-cuda-12.8-x64-avx512_vnni/llama-quantize.exe` | ✅ CUDA 12.8, AVX512_VNNI |

**IMatrix path was stale** — the config still pointed to the old generic
`imatrix-Qwen3.6-27B-BF16.dat` fallback from the initial setup. Updated to
our new code-focused imatrix.

### Recipe verification

Parsed 49 regex rules from recipe file. Coverage:
- **Head/embedding tensors**: 3 rules (output_norm=f32, token_embd=iq3_k, output=iq4_k)
- **Attention norms**: 1 pattern covering all 64 layers → f32
- **Attention weights**: 13 rules covering Q, K, V, QKV, output, gate per layer
- **FFN weights**: 11 rules for up/down/gate per layer
- **SSM tensors**: 15 rules for alpha, beta, dt, out, conv1d, norm, a
- **Post-attention norms**: 1 pattern covering all 64 layers → f32

**--custom-q string length**: 3,243 characters — within Windows 8,191 char limit ✅

### Critical cmd.exe escaping issue

The `--custom-q` regex patterns contain **49 `^` caret characters** (regex
anchors). In cmd.exe, `^` is the **escape character** — typing the command
manually in a Windows terminal would cause every `^` to be consumed by cmd,
completely mangling all 49 regex patterns before llama-quantize even sees them.

**Fix**: Always use `run_local_quant.py` (Python subprocess) which bypasses
cmd.exe by passing arguments directly via CreateProcess. Never type the
llama-quantize command manually in a Windows terminal.

| `--allow-requantize` | Required since source is Q8_0, not BF16/F32 |

## Recipe

The full quantization recipe was generated by [Thireus' GGUF-Tool-Suite](https://github.com/Thireus/GGUF-Tool-Suite) `quant_assign.py`, using KLD sensitivity data from the Qwen3.6-27B reference (same `qwen35` architecture, identical tensor names and shapes).

**Key flags:**
```
--gpu-quants q8_0 iq6_k q6_K iq5_k q5_K iq4_k iq4_ks iq4_xs iq4_kt q4_K ...
--gpu-tensors-max-size 12.92
--tolerance 0.005
--gpu-assign-qtype q6_K
--use-greedy-quant-assign
--harmonization-technique 3
--with-imatrix
```

Recipe file included in this repo: see `quantize/` directory.

## Files

| File | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `Darwin-28B-Coder-IQ4_XS12.9GiB-GGUF.gguf` | The quantized model (12.92 GiB) |
| `custom-darwin-28b-coder.imatrix.dat` | Importance matrix used for quantization (3,200 chunks) |
| `quantize/Darwin-28B-Coder-12.92GiB.recipe.txt` | Full quantization recipe (49 mixed-precision rules) |
| `logs/ppl_darwin-28b-coder-custom-12.92GiB_cfull.log` | Perplexity benchmark log |
| `logs/ppl_reference_q4km_cfull.log` | Reference Q4_K_M perplexity log |

## Usage

### llama.cpp / ik_llama.cpp

```bash
# Basic inference (offload all layers to GPU)
llama-cli -m Darwin-28B-Coder-IQ4_XS12.9GiB-GGUF.gguf -ngl 99

# With MTP speculative decoding (ik_llama.cpp fork)
llama-cli -m Darwin-28B-Coder-IQ4_XS12.9GiB-GGUF.gguf -ngl 99 -mtp --draft-max 2 --draft-p-min 0.80

# Chat mode
llama-cli -m Darwin-28B-Coder-IQ4_XS12.9GiB-GGUF.gguf -ngl 99 -p "<|im_start|>user\nWrite a Python function to merge two sorted lists.<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n"
```

### llama-server

```bash
llama-server -m Darwin-28B-Coder-IQ4_XS12.9GiB-GGUF.gguf -ngl 99 -c 8192 --port 8081
```

### VRAM Notes

On a 16 GiB card this model leaves ~2.9 GiB free. For KV cache:
- **q8_0 KV**: ~2.9 GiB → ~46K context
- **q4_0 KV**: ~2.9 GiB → ~92K context
- **q6_0 KV**: ~2.9 GiB → ~61K context

Use `--cache-type-k` and `--cache-type-v` to adjust KV cache quantization.

## Acknowledgements

- Base model: [VIDraft](https://huggingface.co/VIDraft) for Darwin-28B-Opus and Darwin-28B-Coder
- Finetuning data: [m-a-p](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p) for CodeFeedback Filtered Instruction
- Quantization tools: [Thireus](https://github.com/Thireus) for the GGUF-Tool-Suite and ik_llama.cpp fork
- llama.cpp community for the GGUF format and quantization infrastructure

## Medium Issues

### 1. Unsafe Type Assertions in reconstructCache (index.ts)

**Location:** `reconstructCache()` function, lines ~196-225

Multiple unsafe type casts without validation:

```typescript
const cache = entry.data as typeof cachedExtraction;
const details = (entry.message as any).details;
```

**Risk:** Corrupted session data could cause runtime errors.

**Recommendation:** Add validation before type assertions.

---

### 2. Duplicate Settings Loading (index.ts)

**Location:** `loadAnswerSettings()` called at:
- Tool execution handler (~line 127)
- `/answer` command handler (~line 297)
- `/answer:again` command handler (~line 397)

Settings are loaded from disk each time.

**Recommendation:** Cache settings at extension startup and expose a refresh method.

---

### 3. Inconsistent Field Naming in Cache Reconstruction (index.ts)

**Location:** `reconstructCache()`, lines ~196-225

Two sources with different structures:
- Session entries: `UnifiedQuestion[]`, `lastAssistantEntryId` required
- Message details: `NormalizedQuestion[]`, `lastAssistantEntryId` optional

**Risk:** Subtle bugs when restoring from different sources.

---

### 4. Editor Mode State Not Properly Reset (tui.ts)

**Location:** `loadEditorForCurrentQuestion()`, lines ~186-203

When navigating to a question that doesn't allow Other, `editorMode` is not explicitly reset.

**Risk:** Direct navigation paths may not reset the flag properly.

---

### 5. Magic Array Indices (index.ts)

**Location:** Lines ~380, ~430

```typescript
const a = result.answers[i];
const q = normalizedQuestions[i];  // Relies on index matching
```

**Risk:** If arrays get out of sync, wrong answers returned.

**Recommendation:** Use a map by question ID:
```typescript
const answersById = new Map(result.answers.map(a => [a.id, a]));
```

---

## Low Issues

### 6. Unused Variable: otherQuestionId (tui.ts)

**Location:** Lines ~105, ~660, ~682

## Recall

Pi's default compaction discards old messages permanently — after compaction, the agent only sees the summary. Blackhole preserves searchable history through two surfaces that share the same engine.

### `recall` tool (agent-facing)

The agent can search session history, expand entries, drill into file content, and look up observational memory — all through one tool. Searches read the raw session file directly, bypassing compaction.

| Input | What it does |
|---|---|
| `[12-char hex]` | Recover source evidence for an observation or reflection ID — shows the source entries from the session that backed the observation |
| `#N` | Expand a transcript entry by index (show full content, not truncated) |
| `#N:path` | Drill-down into file content from a tool call (e.g. `#42:auth.ts` shows first 30 lines; `#42:auth.ts:30` shows next 30; `#42:auth.ts:full` shows everything) |
| Free text | BM25-ranked OR search across transcript + file indicators. Rare terms weighted higher. |
| `mode:file` | Search only write/edit file content (not transcript text) |
| `mode:transcript` | Search only conversation text (not file content) |
| `mode:touched` | Aggregate all files written/edited across the session, grouped by path with entry indices |
| Regex | Pattern search (e.g. `fork.*pi-vcc`, `hook|inject`) |
| `scope:all` | Search across all session lineages, not just the active one (default: `lineage`) |

**OM coupling:** When expanding session entries (`#N`), the tool automatically looks up related observations and reflections from the session ledger. If any of your expanded entries are source evidence for an observation, those are shown alongside the expanded content.

### `/blackhole-recall` command (user-facing)

Results are shown as a collapsible message and automatically fed to the agent as context. Same engine as the `recall` tool.

```
/blackhole-recall auth token                        # active-lineage search, ranked
/blackhole-recall auth token page:2                 # paginated (5 results/page)
/blackhole-recall hook|inject                       # regex
/blackhole-recall fail.*build scope:all             # regex across all lineages
/blackhole-recall mode:file                         # search only write/edit file content
/blackhole-recall mode:transcript                   # search only conversation
/blackhole-recall mode:touched                      # aggregate view of all files touched
/blackhole-recall                                   # recent 25 entries
```

### More features

**File drill-down** reads the raw session JSONL to extract file content from tool call operations. Supports offset/limit paging so you can browse long files. Note: edit diffs are not indexed for text search — drill-down reads them from the raw session.

**Touched mode** (`mode:touched`) aggregates all files written, edited, or read across the session, grouped by path. Each entry shows which tool wrote the file and the line count. Useful for getting a lay of the land after a long session.

## Model fallback chains

Each worker has a primary model and an ordered fallback list. On any error — rate limit, timeout, API failure, 5xx — the failed model is cooled down and the next candidate is tried. If all candidates are exhausted, the pipeline aborts and retries on the next trigger event. The session model is always the last resort and is never cooled down.

```
[Worker fails: 429 / timeout / 5xx / connection error]
         │
         v
  Add model to cooldown list
  (persisted to pi-blackhole-cooldown.json)
         │
         v
  Try next fallback candidate
         │
         v
  [All candidates exhausted?]
         │              │
        yes             no ──> try next
         │
         v
  Fall back to session model (never cooled down)
```

Cooldowns survive Pi restarts — they're persisted to `~/.pi/agent/pi-blackhole/pi-blackhole-cooldown.json`. Each entry records the model identifier, the triggering error, which stage failed, and the expiry timestamp.

### Resolution order

For each stage, the runtime builds a candidate list from:

1. **Primary stage model** (`observerModel`, `reflectorModel`, `dropperModel`)
2. **Stage fallback models** (`observerFallbackModels`, etc.) — tried in order
3. **Base model** (`model` — shared across all workers)
4. **Session model** (the model used for your main conversation — always the last resort)

Models with active cooldowns are transparently skipped. The runtime tries up to 10 model resolutions per stage before giving up entirely.

### Example: full resolution chain

With a fully configured setup:

```
Observer:  qwen3-next-80b (openrouter) → gemma4:31b-cloud (ollama) → gemma-4-31b-it:free (openrouter) → base model → session model
Reflector: gpt-oss-120b (cerebras) → glm-4.7 (z.ai) → gpt-oss-120b:free (openrouter) → base model → session model
Dropper:   gpt-oss-120b (cerebras) → glm-4.7 (z.ai) → gpt-oss-120b:free (openrouter) → base model → session model
```

### Per-model thinking levels

Each model config supports a `thinking` field that controls reasoning effort:

```json
{
  "observerModel": {
    "provider": "openrouter",
    "id": "qwen/qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct:free",
    "thinking": "low",       ← reasoning effort for this specific model
    "cooldownHours": 12       ← custom cooldown duration
  }
}
```

Valid values: `off`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`. Not all models support every level.

### Retryable error detection

The runtime uses a regex to detect retryable errors — it looks for patterns like `rate limit`, `429`, `5xx`, `timeout`, `service unavailable`, `connection error`, `websocket closed`, etc. Non-retryable errors (auth failures, invalid model IDs) immediately skip that candidate and move to the next.

### 30-second retry gate

After any stage fails completely, the pipeline waits 30 seconds before attempting another consolidation run. This prevents rapid retry loops that would waste API calls on the same failing models.

---

## Install

```bash
# From npm (recommended)
pi install npm:pi-blackhole

# Or directly from GitHub
pi install git:github.com/k0valik/pi-blackhole
```

If you have standalone pi-vcc or pi-observational-memory installed, remove them first — they will conflict:

```bash
pi uninstall https://github.com/sting8k/pi-vcc
pi uninstall https://github.com/elpapi42/pi-observational-memory
```

Then `/reload` or restart Pi.

### Standalone install (without Pi)

```bash
npm install pi-blackhole
# or
pnpm add pi-blackhole
```

## Uninstall

```bash
pi uninstall git:github.com/k0valik/pi-blackhole
rm -rf ~/.pi/agent/pi-blackhole
```

---

## Credits

The bulk of this codebase comes from two upstream projects:

- **[pi-vcc](https://github.com/sting8k/pi-vcc)** by @sting8k — algorithmic conversation compaction
- **[pi-observational-memory](https://github.com/elpapi42/pi-observational-memory)** by @elpapi42 — session-ledger-based observation and reflection capture

pi-blackhole combines, configures, and extends them into a single extension and adds unified configuration, per-worker model fallback chains, persisted cooldowns, manual flush mode, and conflict resolution between the two, and better error detection.

## 2026-05-22 — Grilling Q4–Q7: naming, scaling, profile format, raw data persistence

### Q4 — Tensor naming across publishers

Tensor names come from the converter (`convert_hf_to_gguf.py`), not from
quantizers. All publishers using the same converter version for the same
architecture should produce identical tensor names. A normalization layer is
a **safety net for converter version mismatches** — rare, but worth handling
gracefully rather than crashing.

### Q5 — Architecture scaling (9B vs 27B vs 35B-MoE)

**Rule:** One profile per exact base model. You inspect Qwen3.5-9B quants to
build a Qwen3.5-9B profile — don't mix 9B and 27B observations.

**Downward generalization only:** A 27B profile *can* be applied to a 9B
fine-tune as a fallback (erring on the safer side — bigger models tend to be
more brittle, so their profiles are conservative). But a 9B profile cannot be
applied upward to a 27B fine-tune.

**No cross-architecture leakage:** A gemma4 profile is only for gemma4.
Qwen3.5 profiles don't apply to Llama.

### Q6 — Profile format, raw data persistence, recipe bridge

**Per-tensor profile statistics** (computed from actual observations, not
heuristics):
- **min_type**: lowest quant type ever assigned (proxy for collapse floor)
- **med_type**: median quant type from observations
- **upper_bound**: highest quant type assigned (the "protected" ceiling)
- **weighted_avg**: weighted average across all observations

**Raw data persistence:**
- `raw/<model_arch>/` — e.g., `raw/qwen35_9b/` — per-model subdirectories
  keep data organized
- `inspect_repo.py` dumps here; aggregators/analyzers read from here
- New repos can be appended later without re-pulling everything
- Re-pulling all data is possible but not preferred; raw files are the
  reproducible source of truth

**Profile → Recipe bridge:** All three approaches combined:
1. Profile is machine-parseable (JSON)
2. A tool generates `quant_assign.py` recipe from it (automated)
3. User can read, verify, and manually adjust the generated recipe

## 2026-05-22 — Grilling session: validation, normalization, regrets

### Grilling outcome — 3 questions aligned

#### Q1: Base → Fine-tune sensitivity transfer

We assume the base model profile is a **conservative floor** for fine-tunes of the
same architecture. Fine-tuning can shift weight distributions either way, but we
err on the safer side by:
- Using the consensus range as default
- Capturing outliers so we can override decisions manually when we have a reason
- Never applying a hard ban — everything is reviewable

**Real-world check from this repo:** The `Omnimerge-v4` quant's recipe had
`output.weight=iq4_k` recommended by the optimizer. User overrode to `iq5_k` as
a "safety patch" — now regretted (+152 MB for no benefit). The optimizer (which
*is* a form of crowd-sourced KLD signal) was right. Lesson: trust the data,
don't add arbitrary safety margins.

#### Q2: Normalization across quant files

We **cannot** rely on quant labels alone — two Q4_K_M files from different
publishers can have different bpw and different per-tensor assignments. We track
all three normalization axes:

1. **Quant label** (Q4_K_M, IQ4_XS, etc.) — coarsest, but most portable
2. **Actual bpw** = file_size_bytes × 8 / total_parameters — computed from
   GGUF header metadata + file size, most precise remotely
3. **File size (GiB)** — straightforward and comparable within same architecture

**New requirement:** Save each repo's README.md as
`<repo_owner>-<model_name>_readme.md` alongside the inspection data. Visual
inspection of publishers' notes, methodology, and known caveats helps interpret
outliers and contested assignments.

#### Q3: Validation before trusting the profile

We already have validation targets in this repo — 3 finished quants with
evaluation data arriving. Use these as ground truth:
1. Take the base model of an existing finished quant
2. Generate a recipe from our crowd-sourced profile at the same bpw
3. Compare KLD/PPL against our existing result
4. If ours is within ~10-20% KLD, the approach is validated

This avoids the trap of generating a recipe for a fine-tune and having no
reference to compare against.

### Edge cases flagged

- **IQ vs K-quant algorithms**: If their underlying quantization methods differ,
the assignments may reflect algorithm preference, not sensitivity. Track this
separately during analysis.
- **Missing bpw normalization**: If a repo only publishes file sizes without
param counts, we may need to fall back to architecture heuristics (known
param_count from model card).
- **Sparse observations**: Some tensors (SSM-specific, adapter layers) may have
very few observations (< 5). These need explicit low-confidence flags in the
profile.

### Why it helps

- **Cache locality**: Processing row N brings rows N+1..N+3 into cache
- **Fewer block headers**: 4 rows share scale metadata → more efficient
- **Better SIMD**: 4 rows' data arranged for vectorized processing

### How to use

```bash
# Quantize normally with V5 recipe
llama-quantize.exe --imatrix imatrix.dat ... -r recipe_darwin_36b_v5_kld_target.txt

# Back up
cp quantized.gguf quantized-original.gguf

# Repack (takes ~2 minutes, zero quality loss)
llama-quantize.exe --only-repack quantized.gguf quantized-r8.gguf
```

The repack operation is handled by `iqk_repack_tensor()` in ik_llama.cpp — pure memcpy + byte rearrangement. No dequantization or requantization occurs, so PPL/KLD are **identical** to the original. Only inference speed (τ/s) changes.

### `token_embd.weight`

This tensor is explicitly excluded from repacking (`is_forbidden_tensor`), so it stays as `iq6_k`. No impact since it's a tiny fraction of the model.

---

## Thireus vs Eaddario: Two Optimization Philosophies

### Thireus (KLD-guided)
- Measures **distribution shift** (KLD) per tensor type from calibration data
- Uses `quant_assign.py` to greedily assign quant types at target size
- **Fast** recipe generation, supports ik_llama.cpp extended types
- **Weakness**: KLD is a proxy — doesn't directly measure quantization error

### Eaddario (target-bpw, error-minimizing)
- Actually quantizes each tensor **15 different ways**, measures error
- Selects best error/size tradeoff at target bpw
- **5-10x slower** but more direct error measurement
- **Weakness**: Per-tensor error is local — ignores cross-layer error propagation

> *"Although the target bpw method produces better quality often (>75% based on tests with 130 models), it can also lose in surprising cases."* — Eaddario

**Our position**: Thireus' KLD recipe for our exact model and target size is the best single reference, but the only true test is to benchmark against the known-good APEX I-Quality at the same size.
